messages.subject: Problems after "Clean and Rebuild"
messages.body_plain:
I just started my first package <https://github.com/arilamstein/choroplethr> on github and some (not all) users are reporting that they cannot run the package after installing it.  I believe that I can reproduce the problem when I click "Clean and Rebuild" and try to run a trivial example:

df = data.frame(region=state.abb, value=sample(100, 50))
choroplethr(df, lod="state")

 Error in generate_values(choropleth$value, num_buckets) :
  could not find function "cut2"

cut2 is in Hmisc is listed as an Import in my DESCRIPTION file, so I'm not sure why it can't be found.  It can be found if I replace "cut2" with "Hmisc::cut2".  I guess the obvious question to ask is this: when writing a package, do all calls to functions from other packages need to include the package name?

After fixing that error I then get another:

    choropleth = ggplot(choropleth, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
                    geom_polygon(aes(fill = value), color = "black") +
                    scale_fill_brewer(scaleName, labels=comma) + # use brewer discrete scale
                    ggtitle(title) +
                    theme_clean();

Error in structure(list(call = match.call(), aesthetics = aesthetics,  :
  object 'comma' not found

I am actually not sure where comma is defined, or why the line above this, which uses plyr, does not cause an error.

Thanks.

Ari

messages.subject: Re: Problems after "Clean and Rebuild"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ari,

Welcome to the wonderful world of namespace debugging. The first tool
to help you is load_all(export_all = FALSE) - this makes load_all()
work more like library(), hiding the functions that are not explicitly
documented. export_all = FALSE makes it easier to iterate as you
figure out which functions need to be imported from other packages.

>From the current messages it sounds like you need something like:

#' @importFrom Hmisc cut2
#' @importFrom scales comma

You'll need to do that for every function you use from another
package. Alternatively, as you discovered you can also skip importing
the function into your namespace and refer to it directly with ::.

Hadley

messages.subject: devtools and github dependencies
messages.body_plain:
I was wondering if anyone has done some work on implementing a system for resolving dependencies that are on Github? As more packages these days are not on CRAN, this problem gets increasingly pressing. I'd really like to add support for this in OpenCPU, one way or another.

Before I start hacking on something myself, I was wondering if any of the 144 forks (?!) has already done something.

messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jeroen,

On 21 Dec 2013, at 06:52, Jeroen Ooms wrote:

> I was wondering if anyone has done some work on implementing a system for resolving dependencies that are on Github? As more packages these days are not on CRAN, this problem gets increasingly pressing. I'd really like to add support for this in OpenCPU, one way or another.
>
> Before I start hacking on something myself, I was wondering if any of the 144 forks (?!) has already done something.

I haven't done anything and I am not aware of particularly relevant work from anyone else. But, I do agree that there is a need to be met here. I had wondered whether this might just as well be achieved by a sort of metapackage website that gathered together information for both CRAN/bioconductor packages as well as in development R packages on github, rforge etc.

Recently I was thinking about what search it would take to find R packages on github automatically – something about repos containing a DESCRIPTION file in their root folder that can be read in by read.dcf etc. Then I happened to notice this:

https://github.com/hadley/r-on-github

So perhaps that could be a source of the location of packages not available on cran/bioc.

Best wishes,

Greg.

messages.subject: Auto versioning packages
messages.body_plain:
The DESCRIPTION file in an R project has a Version field in it.  There seems something a bit incongruous about having that field manually set, though, and having my repo publically available on github.  Arguably every commit should increase the version number since the state of the repository has changed.  My project is fairly new and many days I've had several checkins a day.  One of the primary purposes of version numbers is so that when I get a bug report I can sync to that version to see if I can reproduce the error.  Is there any way to have that number auto increment?

During the advanced r workshop Hadley recommended following the versioning system described in the semantic versioning <http://semver.org/> website.  Has anyone experimented with writing a git hook to autoincrement that number (perhaps with a prompt asking questions which would indicate whether the major/minor/patch version should be increased)?

messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
messages.body_plain:
On Sun, Dec 22, 2013 at 3:15 AM, Gregory Jefferis <jeff...@gmail.com> wrote:
>  by a sort of metapackage website that gathered together information for both CRAN/bioconductor packages as well as in development R packages on github, rforge etc...... Then I happened to notice this: https://github.com/hadley/r-on-github. So perhaps that could be a source of the location of packages not available on cran/bioc.

I doubt this provides reliable foundations for resolving dependencies. You're going to get package name collisions because github does not enforce unique repo names as do cran/bioc. On the contrary: github encourages forking and branching, so there are many versions of one and the same package. I think we should try to support that, rather than inheriting limitations from the cran system.

In my paper in the R journal (http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2013-1/ooms.pdf) I tried to make a case for versioning dependencies. I think we can hit 2 birds with 1 stone by using the github user-repo-branch system. For example, we could introduce some optional file in the source package accompanying the DESCRIPTION file (say: DEPENDENCIES), containing something like (dcf format):

Package: MASS
Version: 7.3-22
URL: http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/MASS/MASS_7.3-22.tar.gz

Package: ggplot2
Version: 0.8.9
URL: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/archive/ggplot2-0.8.9.tar.gz

Package: dplyr
Version: *
URL: https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/archive/master.tar.gz

The default R package manager could simply ignore this file and try to pull MASS, ggplot2 and dplyr from CRAN as defined in DESCRIPTION. But advanced package managers could use information in this file to locate dependencies more carefully, rather than assuming the latest version from cran. E.g. in devtools we can just feed the urls to devtools::install_url() before installing the main package.

The OpenCPU system already uses a separate library for every package installed form github to prevent package version conflicts. So if we could implement some system that resolves dependency packages from specific url/branch rather than cran, that could bring reproducibility a step closer.

Let me know if this sounds sensible/doable/terrible :)

For packman, I was thinking of adding a source field that would work

requested version. I think this is relatively simple, and yet allows
sufficient flexibility. I don't think you want to leave the
DESCRIPTION file if at all possible.

messages.subject: Re: Auto versioning packages
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ari,

I don't think need to update the version number of your package every
time you make a change. The problem is that install_github currently
captures the sha of the exact revision you installed (and saves it in
the DESCRIPTION), but we don't have any tools to surface that detail.
We'll probably add a version of sessionInfo() that also prints that,
which means you only need to increment the version number if you make
an API breaking change.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Auto versioning packages
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Dec 24, 2013 at 1:59 PM,  <arila...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Mon, Dec 23, 2013 at 2:42 PM, Winston Chang <winsto...@gmail.com>
> wrote:
>>
>> One of the problems with incrementing the version number with each
>> commit is that it doesn't work very well with git's distributed model.
>> If all your development is done by a single person on a single branch,
>> then auto-incrementing the version number could work. But if you have
>> multiple people working on a project, then you'll get a lot of merge
>> conflicts with the version number. And if you use branch for
>> development, even by a single person, you'll also get merge conflicts.
>>
>> With the current version of devtools, if someone installs a package
>> with install_github(), it automatically inserts information about the
>> commit and repo into the package description. For example, I've
>> installed shiny from github, and here's what's added:
>> > packageDescription('shiny')
>> [... other stuff trimmed ...]
>> GithubRepo: shiny
>> GithubUsername: rstudio
>> GithubRef: master
>> GithubSHA1: 4e0a61bd9bc94330f8aa1671bf3377bc3b854d1a
>>
>> So you can ask users to provide the hash of the commit when reporting
>> bugs.
>>
>> install() doesn't yet record the commit, but hopefully at some point
>> that will be implemented, so those who clone the repo and install
>> locally will have the SHA.
>>
>> -Winston
>
> Thanks Winston.  That commit hash field will be helpful for me.
>
> I think that I'm struggling to understand how a submission to CRAN should
> relate to what's on github.  Since I have travis-ci integration on github,
> it's arguable that CRAN is irrelevant, since R CMD check and my unit tests
> verify that my latest commit is good.  Can you speak to what advantages
> submitting to CRAN has?  I should say that I just made my first submit 5
> minutes ago.
>
> I'm also unclear about whether the project's homepage on github should
> reflect exactly what's on github or my current development.  After talking
> with some coworkers I think that the best thing is if the master branch
> reflects CRAN, and I create a new branch called development that has my
> intermediary work.
>
> To be honest, I get confused when I see some projects on github that are
> also on cran, because I can't tell which version should be considered
> authoritative.  One thing that's clear is that the CRAN version can never be
> ahead of the github version.  But other than that I'm not sure.
>
> Ari

Oops, I forgot to hit reply-all in my previous message, so I've copied
and pasted the messages above.

The CRAN version of a package is an official release. CRAN has been
around for longer than Github or even git. Sites like Github,
Bitbucket, and R-forge are places where put their in-development code
for packages, but there's no requirement that developers use these
sites.

During development, you might have a changing API, or some
functionality might be broken or partially implemented. Even if you
have unit tests, they may not all pass, or you may have incomplete
coverage. In my experience, the development phase of a project can
often be a churning mess, and only toward the end of a release will
all the little issues get straightened out. For most end users, it's
simpler to just know they need version 0.9 of a project.

You could use the master branch so that it only contains release
versions of your project, but that would be an unusual way to go about
it. A much more common practice with git is to use tags to mark a
particular commit as "v0.9", or something like that.

Hope this helps!
-Winston

messages.subject: Non-automatic vignette with devtools?
messages.body_plain:
https://github.com/wibeasley/RVignetteExample

This is a minimal example of an R package that has a nonstandard vignette. I would like to have a working example of a vignette with these features:
Is built with knitr instead of Sweave.
Uses knitr's code externalization <http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/> feature, where almost all the R code lives in a dedicated *.R file. I've added vignettes/CodeBehindVignette.R to .Rbuildignore, but I don't know if that's necessary.
Is not rebuilt every time the package is checked. I am pretending this vignette takes a long time to run and compile, and should not be run on CRAN or win-builder computer (or even run on the developer's computer is they don't want to take 5+ minutes)
Saves images to a dedicated directory to make it easier to track changes in GitHub. Presumably this directory is ./vignettes/FigureRmd, but the location doesn't really matter to me. I've added this folder to .Rbuildignore, but I'm not sure that's necessary.
I chose an Rmd file instead of a Rnw, so that it could be more portable and run on more development boxes, and increase the chance of getting a more helpful response. If these two types of files handles things differently, I'll add an Rnw example. I am intentionally not using knitr's caching mechanism, in case it makes package development and portability trickier.

I know there were a few tricks to keep the vignettes from being rebuilt automatically, such as placing a stub Rnw file <https://github.com/LiveOak/NlsyLinksStaging/blob/70456b0cd99c77627f338daf977a9fa78cef85b9/NlsyLinks/inst/doc/NlsyAce.Rnw> in the inst/doc directory. But I'm not sure that's legal since R changed the file structure of vignettes (like splitting up the files in the ./vignettes/ and ./inst/doc/). Besides, I'd like to construct them in a consistent way with devtools, to reduce the chance for complications later. I wondering if devtools is planning to do this a different way than the Makefile approach  <http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Writing-package-vignettes>described in R-exts.

Can someone specify a structure that would work naturally with devtools?  If there's an existing resource that describes this, I'd like to know about it. The “Package level documentation” chapter in Advanced R Programming <http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Documenting-packages.html> looks like it was last updated before R 3.0 was released (because it doesn't mention knitr).  I've also looked at R-exts <http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Writing-package-vignettes>, knitr's vignette demo <http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/vignette/>, and older sources like Leisch's 2009 tutorial <http://cran.r-project.org/doc/contrib/Leisch-CreatingPackages.pdf>.  The source for this vignette is on GitHub <https://github.com/wibeasley/RVignetteExample/blob/master/vignettes/>, and can be previewed here <http://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/wibeasley/RVignetteExample/blob/master/inst/doc/CodeBehindVignette.html>.

Thank you, Will Beasley
